His Excellency the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Greece, Mr. George Gerapetritis, and His Excellency the External Affairs Minister of India, Dr. S. Jaishankar. We are privileged to have with us two distinguished UN briefers, Under-Secretary-General and Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies, Amandeep Singh Gill, and Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, Izumi Nakamitsu. I would also like to recognize our cooperation with the Security Council report. in preparing today's event. I warmly welcome its Executive Director, Ms. Marla Candia Thompson, and Mr. Rodrigo Saad, Policy Analyst, whose presentation of Security Council Report's policy paper will provide an important contribution to our discussion. Ladies and gentlemen, we are all witnesses to how artificial intelligence is transforming the tempo of our world. Its extraordinary potential is already apparent, but so too are the profound questions and risks that accompany a technology developing at unprecedented speed in a world where conflict now ignite in any instant and crisis gather force before diplomacy has found its voice. At sea. emerging technologies and artificial intelligence can lift the veil over the vast expanse of the seas and the oceans. They offer new possibilities to enhance maritime domain awareness, early warning and the protection of critical maritime infrastructure. Yet, the same technologies can also introduce new vulnerabilities and risks, reminding us that innovation must always be anchored in international international law with UNCLAWs at its cornerstone. The importance and full applicability of international humanitarian law and international human rights law must also never be overlooked. Today's discussion will allow us to explore both the opportunities these technologies offer and the challenges they present from different perspectives. Without further ado, it is my pleasure to give the floor to His Excellency, Minister Yerasimopoulou. Mr. Minister, you have the floor.

Thank you, Ambassador. Dear colleagues, dear friends, it's a great honor to welcome you today to the joint side event of Greece and India on artificial intelligence, emerging technologies, and international peace and security. I am particularly pleased to co-chair this discussion with my good friend, the Minister of External Affairs of India, Dr. Jaishankar, who's one of the most distinctive personalities in international diplomacy. Let me also warmly thank our distinguished briefers, Amanatip Singh Gill, Izumi Nakamitsu, and Rodrigo Saad. And I would like also to acknowledge the presence of Security Council's Reports Executive Director, Samala Kandian-Thompson. We are going to also discuss the Security Council report, Artificial Intelligence, Geopolitics and the UN Security Council, especially examining the implications of artificial intelligence on peace and security, especially in the maritime domain. Ladies and gentlemen, artificial intelligence is already transforming the international security environment. It offers significant opportunities to strengthen our ability to prevent conflict, protect civilians, and support peace. At the same time, it creates new vulnerabilities and raises profound questions about responsibility, accountability, and the application of international law. The question before us is therefore no longer whether AI will affect international peace and security. It already does. The question is how we choose to shape that transformation. For Greece, the starting point is clear. Artificial intelligence must remain human-centered, responsible, and firmly anchored in international law. The UN Charter, international humanitarian law, and international human rights law remain fully applicable as technologies evolve. And one principle should remain constant. Technology can augment human judgments, but it cannot replace human responsibility. Important international initiatives have already contributed to this discussion, including the RAIAM process, the political declaration on responsible military use of artificial intelligence and autonomy, and the India AI Impact Summit earlier this year. Greece has also sought to advance this conversation with the United Nations. In April 2025, together with France and the Republic of Korea, we convened an ARIM formula meeting of Security Council on artificial intelligence and international peace and security. Today, we want to take this discussion further, with particular attention to the maritime domain. The opportunities are considerable. AI can strengthen maritime domain awareness and early warning. contribute to safer navigation and shipping and enhance the protection and resilience of critical maritime infrastructure. More fundamentally, it can help us move from reaction towards anticipation, identifying emerging threats earlier, understanding them better, and responding before they escalate. But AI is also inherently dual use. Capabilities developed for legitimate and peaceful purposes have indeed vulnerabilities affecting port, shipping, critical infrastructures and undersea cables. The maritime domain therefore provides a compelling illustration of both the promise and the risk associated with artificial intelligence. I would also like to acknowledge India's long-standing contribution to discussions on science and technology in the context of international security through its annual initiative in the first committee this morning. We had first gathering of the Group of Friends of Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, where my good friend, Dr. Jay Sanka, led the initiative alongside with the Foreign Minister of Liberia. For Greece, maritime security has been a central priority throughout our tenure on the Security Council. We have sought to keep the protection of maritime routes and critical infrastructure, and above all, the safety and security of seafarers, firmly on the Council's agenda. As Greece prepares to assume the presidency of the Security Council in October, we believe that the Council should look not only at the risk created by new technologies, but also at how they can strengthen our collective capacity for prevention and peace. Let me highlight in this respect four considerations. First, we should harness AI as a tool for prevention. AI can strengthen early warning and conflict analysis, support peace operations, facilitate mediation and humanitarian response, and improve maritime situational awareness. The ambition should not simply be to manage crises more efficiently. It should be to anticipate them earlier and, where possible, prevent them. Secondly, we need stronger partnerships. Governments and international organizations do not possess all the technology or expertise required to understand this transformation. We need stronger cooperation with technology companies, the scientific community and academia based on clear responsibilities and appropriate safeguards. When it comes to maritime security, we need to also engage with the maritime community. Thirdly, our multilateral institutions must keep pace with technological change. The Security Council should be able to consider the implications of emerging technologies more systematically when they affect international peace and security, drawing more regularly on scientific and technical expertise. And finally, innovation must go hand in hand with responsibility. And this is the most critical factor of my presentation. The opportunities offered by AI cannot come at the expense of international law, human oversight and accountability. There are no obstacles to innovation. They are conditions for trust. And the truth is that the artificial intelligence is not another phase of industrial revolution. It's a new industrial revolution. And the idea is that for the first time, I think there is a direct challenge towards the supremacy of human brain. The positive things we all understand and know, health, education, growth applications, obviously addressing global challenges such as climate crisis. However, there is a significant risk and this comes through the possible under regulation or unchecked implementation of artificial intelligence. First of all, the impact on vulnerable groups and especially children cannot go unattended. Secondly, massive job destructions. We expect to have a transformation of the labor market as AI proceeds immensely. Thirdly, concentrated wealth. Obviously, since AI will develop technologies that will be at large scale marketable, it's obvious that this will produce profits. And in this respect, we can expect global inequalities already existing at large scale to become greater. Now, we shouldn't, in my eyes, have an illusion that artificial intelligence operators can indeed self-regulate. This is something that I cannot believe and expect. We need strong regulation when it comes to AI. Strong regulation concerning license, concerning supervision, concerning a sanction system for possible violations of fundamentals concerning the implementation of artificial intelligence, and most importantly, a very powerful international regulator to actually see how artificial intelligence progress to the benefit of humanity and not to the benefit of specific humans. Technology will continue to evolve. The question for us is whether our institutions, our cooperation, and our collective ambition can evolve with it. And this is a conversation we want to advance today, and one that Greece and India intends to carry forward within the United Nations. Thank you.
Thank you, Minister. I kindly invite Dr. S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister of India, for his opening remarks.

Thank you. Co-Chair and my good friend, Minister Gerapetritis, Under-Secretary-General Amandeep Singh Gill, Under-Secretary-General Izumi Nakamitsu, Mr. Rodrigo Saad, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues. I'm honored today to co-chair this discussion with Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis on a subject that is both increasingly consequential and rapidly evolving. Artificial intelligence is transforming our economies, our societies, and inevitably, our security environment. The question before us is therefore no longer whether AI will have implications for international peace and security, but how we harness its possibilities, anticipate its consequences, and mitigate its risks. This requires balance. An approach driven exclusively by apprehension risks constraining innovation and denying its benefits, particularly to developing countries. But An approach that ignores the security implications of AI would be equally short-sighted. This February, we hosted the AI Impact Summit. The New Delhi Declaration was premised on a simple proposition. The promise of AI can be realized fully only when its benefits are shared by humanity. Its emphasis on democratizing access to AI resources building secure and trustworthy systems, investing in human capabilities, and using AI for economic growth and social good reflected the concerns and aspirations of countries at very different stages of technology development. At the same time, we must also recognize that AI has a clear security dimension. It can improve early warning and situational awareness, It can strengthen peacekeeping and humanitarian operations. It can support conflict analysis. It can enable faster and better informed decisions. But it can also amplify cyber threats, facilitate disinformation, enhance autonomous capabilities, and lower barriers for malicious actors. Now, nowhere is this duality more evident than in the maritime domain. Recent conflicts have demonstrated how disruption at critical maritime choke points have consequences that are far beyond their immediate region. Attacks on commercial shipping affect not merely the parties to the conflict, but food security, energy security, and economic stability across the world. Artificial intelligence can enhance maritime domain awareness by processing large volumes of satellite, radar, and vessel tracking data. It can improve anomaly detection, assist search and rescue operations, strengthen disaster response, identify suspicious maritime activity, and enhance the resilience of ports and other critical infrastructure. Our Information Fusion Center for the Indian Ocean region, which is located just outside Delhi, works with partners to strengthen maritime domain awareness and information sharing. But as I pointed out, these same technologies also create vulnerabilities. AI can be used for sophisticated reconnaissance, vulnerability mapping, and cyber operations against ports, vessels, communication networks, and undersea infrastructure. Increasing autonomy in maritime systems raises questions of attribution, accountability, and escalation, while also compressing decision-making time. We therefore need an approach that preserves human responsibility and accountability. International law, including the UN Charter, and the laws of seas as reflected in UNCLOS remain the essential framework governing state conduct. Their application must be consistent with existing international obligations. These considerations also underlined by AI governance cannot be reduced to regulation alone. We need greater transparency, confidence building, capacity development, technical cooperation, and exchange of best practices. Developing countries must have the capability to assess AI systems, protect their infrastructure, and participate meaningfully in the shaping of norms. Friends, colleagues, the United Nations has an important role in building that common ground. Different UN bodies have distinct mandates and expertise. Discussions on AI should reinforce rather than duplicate them. In the Security Council, the focus should appropriately remain on those applications and consequences of AI that have a demonstrable bearing on international peace and security. India will bring precisely this approach to the Security Council if elected for the 2028-29 term. As I stated when we launched our candidature earlier this year, We seek a world where the promise of technology is fully realized while safeguarding against its misuse and application, and where our oceans remain safe and secure so that maritime lifelines are not threatened. AI and maritime security will therefore both be important priorities for India during our Security Council term. We would seek to promote practical discussions focused on building capacities sharing experiences, strengthening resilience, and developing a clearer understanding of emerging risks, rather than creating new divisions or imposing prescriptions. Our objective should therefore be to ensure that AI strengthens human security rather than undermines it, that it expands opportunity rather than inequality, and that it helps to make our shared maritime commons safer rather than more contested. So I look forward to hearing the perspectives of our distinguished briefer and to a very productive exchange this afternoon. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Mr. I now invite the Under Secretary General and Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies, Mr. Amarjeet Singh Gill, for his briefing. You have the floor.

Thank you very much. Good afternoon, everyone, Your Excellency. Minister of Foreign Affairs of Greece, Your Excellency Dr. Jaishankar, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Minister of India. It's an honor to be convoked to this meeting, co-hosted by two nations with a great maritime tradition. I will confine my remarks to the non-military aspects of this issue, given, Minister, your exhortation that We have these different mandates, different responsibilities, and we need to work together in that spirit. And I'm sure Izumi will get into that aspect. Now, recently in July, I had the opportunity of being on a fully autonomous yacht. And this was right after a ride in a fully autonomous flying drone. So these technologies are no longer science fiction. They are a part of daily life. And there's tremendous potential in the maritime domain, parking ships safely and in a fast manner in congested ports, the safety and security of seafarers, sustainability of fossil fuel use, and many, many other areas in the maritime space will benefit, I'm sure, from AI. Likewise, there are risks, even though in the maritime domain, the risk of collateral damage is sometimes more manageable than it is on land, but still there are plenty of risks that we have to contend with. There are in the non-military domain, risks around counterterrorism, cybersecurity, other areas where non-state actors are particularly active. And we've seen that in many maritime areas. Experience with piracy on the high seas is just one example. So if you look back at the Global Digital Compact, the the focus is on the non-military domain, but there is this overlap with peace and security issues. And the Secretary-General's attempt has been to, through his own office and otherwise, to bring a whole of UN perspective to these issues, because technology doesn't sit in one place, it travels, it affects different domains. And this technology in particular is not just dual use, but it is repurposeable in different ways. And it is combinatorial, can come together with other technologies for novel effects. So what is happening at the UN is this coordinated approach, part of which is improving our own work inside the UN, UN 2.0, using AI and other emerging technologies for greater efficiency, better delivery of humanitarian action on the ground, better delivery on our mandates given by member states. And then there is an external facing role which has a policy dimension. And you see that illustrated in the work of the new mechanisms that have been created through the Global Digital Compact, the UN's independent international scientific panel on AI, 40 global experts from around the world who are giving regular independent assessments of the direction, the pace, the opportunities and the risks related to this technology. On 1st July, in their preliminary report, they said that the possibility of these autonomous agents acting beyond human, explicit human instructions could not be ruled out. And just 10 days later, that was borne out by this incident where these agents escaped their sandbox and compromised the cybersecurity of a significant platform. And now we see there have been other such incidents. So the panel's work is important. And earlier this week, early morning on Monday, 5 a.m., they released a thematic brief focused on this particular incident and what it implies for multilateral cooperation. And this resonated at the Security Council as well. just a couple of days ago, when many of the tech companies involved in these developments, including the victim and the perpetrator of this attack, brief the Security Council and in fact, in a somewhat surprising turn, asked the international community to come together and address these risks as a matter of priority. The Security Council was also briefed by the co-chair of the independent panel, Dr. Joshua Now, going forward, there is another meeting of the panel that will happen at the end of November in Barbados, and there is a request from the panel to convene with leaders from these frontier model companies, the representatives of AI safety institutes and other independent experts. Minister, you mentioned the importance of capacity around safety testing should be available everywhere. So this discussion would move along. given the urgency of the issue. And next year, there'll be the global dialogue, second global dialogue on AI governance in May in New York. I think there are three areas, and I want to close with this, three areas where we need to connect the dots and make sure that multilateral cooperation is focused on those three areas. One is the travel from the evidence to the policy. So the panel's remit is policy relevant, but not policy prescriptive advice, and Member States have to take forward the policy actions in the dialogue and in other forums in the multilateral space. The other bridge we need to cross is on capacity. So science and policy are important, but without capacity, they remain abstract. So capacity is not only a development imperative, it's also a governance imperative. So you need these assessment capabilities, even whether you buy, borrow, or build AI, you need those capacities. So we need to translate from the AI divide to this capacity lift. And finally, I think we need to make the connection to the existing bedrock of norms. International humanitarian law has been mentioned, IMO conventions have been mentioned. So there's no need to reinvent the wheel. Some of the suggestions made in the Security Council, for example, if you rely on the bedrock of existing norms, then you can make the translation to this domain seamlessly without duplication and without taking away sovereignty from national implementation authorities, national regulatory authorities. So we look forward to working on those areas of urgent importance. Thank you so much.
For his most informative briefing and I invite the Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs, Ms. Yumi Nakamitsu, for her briefing.

Thank you very much, Madam Ambassador. Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, dear colleagues, it is indeed a privilege to join you today to discuss artificial intelligence in the context of international security, with an emphasis on maritime security. And I would like to extend my sincere gratitude to their excellencies, Minister Gera Petricis and Minister Jayashenka, for their leadership in convening this very timely side event. It is, of course, no longer news to anyone that AI affects everyone and every aspect of our lives, and it will continue to be the case. International peace and security, of course, is no exception. Militaries and increasing militaries are increasingly integrating AI across a wide range of functions. the accelerated pace of technological development must be matched by effective governance, safeguards, and international cooperation to ensure that human agency, judgment, and control are preserved as these systems become more agentic. Specifically in the context of maritime security, AI presents both opportunities and, of course, risks. So let me begin with the opportunities. AI can improve maritime domain awareness by analyzing large volumes of information from satellites, radar, sonar, and other maritime tracking systems. For states responsible for large maritime areas, These capabilities can support more effective monitoring and improve the detection of illicit or suspicious activities. AI can also support search and rescue, early warning, monitoring and verification, and the implementation of relevant Security Council measures as well. Other emerging technologies may strengthen these applications. Advances in position, navigation and timing, for example, could help AI enabled and autonomous systems operate when satellite based signals are disrupted and unavailable. But the same technologies could also introduce new security risks. Let me mention a couple of them. First, Uncrewed surface and undersea vessels are proliferating rapidly among militaries, changing the character of maritime operations. AI is particularly attractive enabling technology for these vehicles, allowing them to operate with greater autonomy, over longer distances and for longer periods, including in environments where communications may be limited or disrupted. Greater autonomy and speed may reduce the time available for human assessment and intervention, while interactions between AI-enabled autonomous systems could increase risks of misperception, miscalculation, or unintended escalation. This makes it particularly important to preserve human judgment and control over the use of force. Second, AI is changing what can be observed at sea. As the ability to detect, classify, and track military activities improves, states may reassess the vulnerabilities of their own forces. This becomes particularly consequential where nuclear weapons are involved. These developments, whether actual or perceived, have the potential to undermine strategic stability and create use it or lose it mentalities about nuclear weapons, raising the prospect for first strikes. More broadly, the potential integration of AI into early warning systems or nuclear weapons systems create additional risks. The former increases prospects for spoofing, hacking, or misidentification, leading to increased prospects for mistake or miscalculation and escalation. The latter, that is the nuclear weapons systems, The Secretary General has been very clear. Humanity's fate must not be left to an algorithm. Pending their total annihilation, humans must remain in control of nuclear weapons at all times. Now, third, AI-enabled maritime systems depend on an increasingly complex digital ecosystem. This creates dependencies and potential vulnerabilities. Submarine cables are a load-bearing part of this digital infrastructure. Recent incidents in which such cables were cut, whether accidentally or on purpose, have highlighted both their importance and their vulnerabilities. In addition, global navigation satellite system, GNSS, Jamming or spoofing incidents have already been documented in the Black Sea, Persian Gulf, and around contested waters in the Asia-Pacific region. These opportunities and risks point to the same conclusion. AI becomes more deeply integrated into maritime domain, governance and safeguards must evolve alongside technological capabilities. Though its two resolutions on the through its two resolutions on AI in the military domain, the General Assembly has actually begun a process that has thus far yielded a report of the sector general in 2025 last year and a fruitful informal exchanges earlier this year. At the same time, the efforts of Greece and others have shown there is a role for the Security Council as well. At a minimum, this entails keeping abreast of technological developments and their impact on Security Council mandated sanctions regimes and on situations on its agenda. Given the Security Council's primary responsibility for international peace and security, it could also play a more strategic role should it so choose. There has been a great interest among Council members to regularize engagement on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence. The UN Office for Disarmament Affairs is always available to support such efforts. We are navigating turbulent times. Military expenditure is increasing. Mistrust is spreading. and the risks of miscalculation and escalations are growing. Rapid technological challenge adds another layer of complexity to this environment. So together, we can ensure that advancements in science and technology serve rather than undermine the purposes and principles of this organization and, of course, the humankind overall. I trust that today's discussion will be a positive step forward. I'm looking forward to the exchanges that will follow. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Under-Secretary-General Nakamitu, for your very pertinent briefing. And now, I would like to introduce the Executive Director of the Security Council Report, Ms. Amala Candia-Thompson, for her briefing. Thank you.

I get to do a short introduction, whereas my colleague will have to do the bigger briefing. But, Excellencies, distinguished guests, dear colleagues, on behalf of Security Council Report, I would like to thank the governments of Greece and India for organizing this event today. It is an honor for us to be able to launch our policy paper at this important event, and I would particularly like to express our gratitude to Greece for supporting the paper. For those of you who may not be familiar with SCR, we are an independent and impartial think tank dedicated to the transparency and effectiveness of the Security Council. For over 20 years, we've provided information and independent analysis of the Council's work through our regular publications, as well as in-depth reports. Our research reports have tended to focus on thematic issues that are significant in the work of the Council. And as the international peace and security landscape evolves, we have begun devoting greater attention to emerging challenges that we see affecting the Council's work. In March, we published a research report that examined the Council's engagement with new and emerging technologies, including information and communication technologies and AI, and identified options for strengthening engagement in these areas. Our policy paper, which is titled, "Artificial Intelligence, Geopolitics, and the UN Security Council," builds on that research, providing a more focused examination of AI's implications for international peace and security, and the council's role in addressing it. I'll leave it to my colleague, Rodrigo, who was the author of this paper and our research report, to provide you with the details of the paper. but I hope that the policy paper will provide a useful resource for Council members and the wider UN membership for continued engagement on this rapidly evolving issue. Thank you.
And now I give the floor to the author of the report, Mr. Rodrigo Saad.

Thank you, Madam Ambassador, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, dear colleagues. I would like to thank Greece and India for convening this event and Shyamala for her kind introduction. We tend to think of artificial intelligence as something that lives in the cloud, but in practice, it rests on the sea. The minerals, the semiconductors, and the computing equipment that AI depends on travel by ship. The data that connects AI systems across borders travels through cables on the ocean floor. The relationship runs in both directions. AI is changing what states and non-state actors are able to do at sea for those who protect the maritime domain and for those who threaten it. That is why the paper we are launching today, Artificial Intelligence, Geopolitics, and the UN Security Council, runs maritime security through it as a thread to show how AI intersects with issues already before the council. Greece and India have each brought maritime security before the Council at the highest political level. Greece last year in a debate chaired by its Prime Minister and India in 2021, when the Council adopted its first product devoted to maritime security. In 2024, the Council committed to taking scientific advances into account more systematically, where appropriate and within its mandate. So my question today is a practical one: how can the Council build on those commitments? To answer that, we have to start with the competition now surrounding this technology. Expectations about where the technology is heading are shaping investment and strategic decisions today. That includes the prospect of systems matching or exceeding human performance across a broad range of tasks, what is often called artificial general intelligence. And this competition extends well beyond the technology itself. Advanced AI depends on semiconductors, computing infrastructure, energy, data, and critical minerals. And these resources and capabilities are unevenly distributed. Many developing countries supply essential minerals, while advanced computing infrastructure and model development remain concentrated elsewhere. Resource producing countries are seeking a greater share of the value created, the chance to develop their own capabilities, and a voice in how AI is governed. This has consequences for peace and security. In fragile and conflict-affected settings, rising demand for minerals can reinforce conflict economies where extraction finances armed groups. Disputes over access, ownership, and revenue sharing can shape the incentives of conflict parties and prolong hostilities. It also runs through the maritime domain. More than 80% of international trade in goods by volume travel by ship. And where production is already concentrated, a disruption at a single choke point compounds the exposure. Beneath the sea, some 500 cables carry more than 99% of international data traffic. Three or four are damaged somewhere in the world every week, mostly by anchors and fishing gear. But recent incidents have raised concerns about deliberate damage. But AI is already shaping peace and security in more immediate ways, and not only for the worse. The UN is applying AI to its peace and security work. It has used AI-enabled digital technologies to consult large numbers of people in their own languages, including in support of peace processes. Missions are also using AI-enabled tools to analyze online discourse and radio broadcasts for harmful narratives directed at civilians and at the missions themselves. Situational awareness platforms such as UNITE Aware bring mission data together into a single operational picture. UNITE Aware was launched in this building during India's Council presidency in August 2021. At that same meeting, the Council recognized that technology can act as a force multiplier in peacekeeping for the safety of peacekeepers and for the protection of civilians through better early warning and more timely decisions. AI could extend that commitment. Applied to the data missions already hold, it could help assess where violence is likely to occur and inform patrol planning. Similar capabilities could support mediation, ceasefire monitoring, sanctions monitoring, and conflict analysis, much of the Council's existing toolkit. The effective use of these tools depend on the quality of the data missions record. They depend on the personnel able to judge the outputs, including when the outputs are wrong. And they depend on protecting sensitive information. A decade ago, a UN expert panel found that UN peacekeeping was, quote unquote, "well behind the curve on technology" and introduced the idea of a digital peacekeeper. The question now is whether we are moving towards something closer to an agentic peacekeeper, systems that can automatically monitor sources, cross-check claims, and keep assessments current. But this is not a substitute for personnel. I would make the opposite point, in fact, to take the repetitive work off them so that judgment, political analysis, and relationships with local communities receive more of their time. and humans must retain meaningful oversight of these tools. In corporate evaluations, misaligned model behavior has done limited damage. Inside a peacekeeping mission, the damage would not be so contained. The capabilities that support this work are also becoming available to actors seeking to undermine it. Generative AI lowers the barriers to activities that once required expertise, greater expertise, and resources. UN sanctions monitoring has documented terrorist groups using AI to produce and translate propaganda and to seek guidance on improvised explosive devices and target selection. Just this month, Anthropic reported that threat actors in northern Yemen had used its models across three guided weapons programs. The actors test fired a guided rocket, and when it failed, they went back to the model to diagnose the fault. The same report describes blocked attempts to use the models for research that could support biological weapons development, a concern squarely within the remit of the Council's 1540 Committee. The same dynamic runs through cybersecurity. Capable coding models and AI agents now let a single operator run campaigns that until recently required a full team. In that same anthropic report, one state-linked group ran an AI-driven espionage operation against a government agency responsible for maritime shipping and tracking. The same capabilities work for defenders. AI can find and fix vulnerabilities as quickly as it can exploit them, which matters most for countries with the least cybersecurity capacity. Generative AI is also changing the information environment in which diplomacy and conflict unfold. Fabricated images, video, or audio could suggest that a ceasefire has been broken or that a leader has ordered an attack. Such material circulates before authenticity can be established, potentially fueling violence and undermining mediation. Then there's military decision making. AI is being used to sift intelligence at volume and to help identify targets. That compresses the time commanders have to verify, and under pressure, people tend to trust what the machine tells them. Just last week, CNN reported that earlier this year, an AI-assisted intelligence assessment concluded that a foreign vessel in the Middle East was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. And according to four sources, the military prepared to board the ship. Aircraft were already in the air. Only then did officials examine how the assessment had been produced and found that a chatbot had misidentified the cargo. One source said the report almost started a war. That operation was a maritime interdiction. The delegation of decisions involving lethal force raises further questions. Autonomous weapons are already in use, where systems select and engage targets without further human intervention. Questions of accountability and compliance with international humanitarian law follow. Peace operations must work in environments increasingly shaped by AI amplified risks, cyber attacks on missions and host country systems, drones and autonomous weapons that endanger personnel, disinformation that erodes trust with local communities and complicates mandate delivery. Missions need the capabilities to operate safely in that environment. A further concern raises from the behavior of these systems themselves. During evaluations, AI agents have bypassed restrictions, attacked real third party systems, and concealed what they were doing. Two days ago, Australian authorities disclosed that in June, an OpenAI agent had hacked the government health statistics portal, accessing non-public files. This is the first known case of an AI agent breaching a government system. The company said that its model had taken unintended actions and notified the Australian government three months later. More capable agents behaving this way could cause serious harm. If one gained access to critical infrastructure or to control over physical systems of vessel at sea or port, the consequences would not be confined to the digital environment. These AI systems are also increasingly used to build the next generation of models, a process recursive self-improvement. If that continues, capabilities may advance faster than we can understand them, and meaningful human control becomes harder to maintain. That is why testing, independent oversight, and incident reporting matter now, and why on Wednesday the companies building these systems came to the council asking for rules. But competition between companies and between states rewards speed over caution. Arrangements of that kind need the wider international community. The Council's contribution should be grounded in its mandate. There are political differences about how that contribution should go. Many favor more sustained engagement. Other questions whether broad discussions of AI belong in a body of 15 members and caution against treating AI primarily as a security issue. That disagreement was audible in the Council chamber as recently as Wednesday. Those differences make agreement on new formal mechanisms unlikely in the new term. They also make complementarity with the wider UN system more important. But the technology will continue to advance, and so will its effect on peace and security. The Council's engagement thus has to advance along with it. Two things make that difficult. The first is sustained attention. There's no dedicated agenda item on AI and no standing reporting cycle. The Council has held four formal meetings on AI to date. Each of those happened at the initiative of individual members. But the presidency changes every month, and elected members leave after two years. Nothing reliably carries the analysis across those transitions. The second gap is access to information. The expertise exists within the UN system in missions, sanctions panels, counterterrorism bodies. as well as among researchers and practitioners outside the UN. What members lack is a standing form that brings it together at the point where it bears on decisions that the Council is taking. The main option the paper puts forward to address these gaps is an informal expert group on technology, peace and security. Let me describe exactly what that would entail. Council experts meet out of public view a few weeks before a vote on a draft resolution or a mandate renewal. They are briefed by people who know the subject from within and beyond the UN system. They get to ask the briefers questions. They work out what the technology means for the situation in front of them. And then they take that back to their delegations before negotiations begin. The Council has done this before with issues that once sat at the edges of its work. The Expert Group on the Protection of Civilians was created in 2009 at the initiative of the UK and meets ahead of mandate renewals with the protection dimension. The Group on Women, Peace and Security followed in 2016. In both cases, the purpose was the same, to take a cross-cutting thematic issue that was raised occasionally and make it a routine part of the Council's work. That is a task with technology now. Take maritime security. Such a group could bring sanctions, sanctions experts together with specialists in maritime monitoring and ask how AI might help identify illicit activity at sea and how it might help conceal it. Thank you, Ambassador. Excellencies, dear foreign ministers, dear undersecretaries, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen. Allow me, as we bring this event to a close, to thank all participants for timely and valuable discussion on AI and international peace and security. I think that our discussion has underlined that AI is reshaping the global security landscape. It creates new opportunities to improve situational awareness, strengthen early warning capabilities, support crisis management, and protect critical infrastructure. Especially in the maritime domain, AI can enhance maritime awareness, identify suspicious activity, improve navigation safety, and help vast maritime areas more effectively than even before. At the same time, AI can also amplify existing risks, including cyber threats, disinformation, and the misuse of autonomous systems. These opportunities and risks must continue to be addressed together. For Greece, AI is a strategic enabler that's already transforming the maritime security environment, strengthening both maritime domain awareness and the protection and resilience of critical maritime infrastructure. Given Greece's operational presence across the Eastern Mediterranean, the wider Mediterranean, and the Middle East, AI enables the fusion and analysis of vast volumes of satellite, radar, automatic identification systems, radio frequencies, and other data to identify anomalous behavior, dark or shadow vessels, illicit activities, and migration flows, supporting earlier responses and ultimately saving lives at the sea. A key conclusion from today's exchange is that these capabilities must be employed in full respect of the UN Charter, of course, UNCLOS, and the established rules of international law and the law of the sea, which provide the common legal framework for all states and all activities at sea. For Greece, responsible use of AI should reinforce, not weaken, freedom of navigation, respect of sovereign rights, and the rule of international law. The maritime dimension has rightly received particular attention. Growing dependence on undersea cables, ports, logistic networks, and other critical maritime infrastructure creates new vulnerabilities. AI can be used for reconnaissance, vulnerability identification, and increasingly sophisticated cyber operations. Yet, the same technology can strengthen resilience through predictive maintenance, anomaly detection, cyber defense, and real-time monitoring of maritime activities. As a country with the world's largest merchant fleet and a strong maritime tradition, Greece views the protection of maritime infrastructure as a strategic priority. This is why Greece's national approach combines innovation with governance. We have established the Special Secretariat for AI and Data Governance, implementing the national law for the EU AI Act, and we are investing in strategic infrastructure, including the Vethalos supercomputer and the Pharos AI factory. These initiatives reflect our commitment to trustworthy, secure, and human-centric AI. As we conclude, the United Nations has a vital role to play in promoting dialogue, exchanging best practices, strengthening capacity building, supporting international cooperation, and ensuring coherence across security, development, human rights, and technology governance. No country can address these challenges alone. The responsible governance of AI requires a multilateral engagement, shared principles, and collective action. Let this be the message with which we close today's event. AI must serve peace, security, resilience, and sustainable development firmly anchored in international law and human values. Thank you.
